description: Mission and evangelism for Catholics today, the aims of the SVP, and the work of either Corrymeela or Pax Christi.
content_html:
What Is Mission?

Mission is the task given by the risen Jesus to his followers: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20). This command, known as the Great Commission, is foundational to Catholic identity. The Catholic Church understands itself as a missionary Church — not in the sense of imposing its beliefs on others, but in the sense that it has something of great importance to offer: the Good News of God’s love and the invitation to share in the life of Christ.

Evangelism (or evangelisation) is the process of sharing the Good News. For Catholics today in Britain, evangelism takes many forms: inviting friends and neighbours to Mass, running faith exploration courses (such as RCIA — the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults), speaking openly about faith in workplaces and schools, and engaging in dialogue with people of other faiths. Pope Francis has consistently urged Catholics to be a “missionary Church” — one that reaches out rather than waiting for people to come to it.

Key Fact

The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20): Jesus commands his disciples to “go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” This is the foundation of Catholic mission: the Gospel is not private property but a gift to be shared with everyone. Catholics in Britain today engage in evangelism through faith courses, parish outreach and community service.

The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP)

The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP) was founded in Paris in 1833 by a group of young Catholic university students led by Frédéric Ozanam. It is named after St Vincent de Paul (1581–1660), a French priest who dedicated his life to the service of the poor and who reformed the training of priests and the care of the sick and orphaned in seventeenth-century France.

The SVP is an international lay organisation operating in 153 countries. Its members — called Vincentians — visit people in their homes, hospitals and care homes, offer practical help (food parcels, clothing, furniture), befriend the lonely and isolated, and run projects for the homeless, the unemployed and those in financial difficulty. The SVP operates through local parish conferences (groups), making it one of the most locally embedded Catholic charitable organisations in Britain. Its motto is “Serviens in Spe” — “Serving in Hope.”

What distinguishes the SVP from purely secular charities is its emphasis on the personal relationship: Vincentians do not simply deliver goods, they sit with the people they serve, treating each person as Christ. The theological grounding is Matthew 25:40: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” In a Catholic parish in Liverpool, for example, the local SVP conference might visit elderly parishioners who cannot attend Mass, bring Holy Communion to the housebound, run a lunch club for the lonely, and collect food for a local food bank.

Pax Christi (Latin: “Peace of Christ”) is an international Catholic peace movement founded in 1945, initially as a movement of Franco-German reconciliation after the Second World War. It now works in over forty countries, campaigning for disarmament (including opposition to nuclear weapons), challenging militarism, and promoting reconciliation between enemies as a concrete expression of the Gospel.

Pax Christi’s theological foundation is the Beatitude “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9) and the Catholic commitment to the “just war” tradition alongside its increasingly strong pacifist strand. In Britain, Pax Christi UK campaigns against the Trident nuclear weapons programme, works with schools on peace education, and runs interfaith peace-building initiatives. The organisation sees disarmament not as political preference but as a moral requirement flowing from the sanctity of human life and the command to love one’s enemy (Matthew 5:44).

The Corrymeela Community is an ecumenical Christian reconciliation community in Northern Ireland, founded in 1965 by Ray Davey — a Presbyterian minister who had been a prisoner of war and had witnessed the destruction of Dresden. Located at a residential centre on the Antrim coast, Corrymeela brings together Catholics and Protestants divided by the violence of the Troubles, young people from different communities, and families affected by conflict, to work together on healing and understanding.

Corrymeela is notable for being explicitly Christian but ecumenical — it does not belong to one denomination. Its work is grounded in the conviction that the Gospel calls all Christians to reconciliation, drawing on Paul’s letter to the Corinthians: “All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18). While primarily Protestant in origin, the GCSE specification names Corrymeela alongside Pax Christi as an example of Catholic-engaged peace-building, because it works across the Catholic-Protestant divide and many Catholics participate in its work.

Catholics in Great Britain: Mission Today

There are approximately five million Catholics in England and Wales, making Catholicism the largest single Christian denomination. Catholics in Britain today engage in mission in a context very different from earlier centuries: a secular, pluralist society in which faith is often treated as a private matter. The challenge of Catholic mission in Britain is therefore not primarily overseas but local: how to share the Gospel with a society that is largely unchurched, and how to demonstrate the relevance of Catholic teaching and practice to contemporary life.

This local mission takes many forms. Westminster Cathedral in London hosts regular public events, concerts, lectures and open days to engage people who might not otherwise encounter Catholicism. Individual parishes run Alpha and RCIA courses for people exploring the faith. The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales speaks publicly on issues of justice, education and family life, acting as a public voice for Catholic Social Teaching in national debate. For Catholics, none of this is separate from the central command: “Love the Lord your God… and love your neighbour as yourself” (Matthew 22:37–39).

Key Fact

SVP: international lay organisation visiting and serving the poor person-to-person in 153 countries, grounded in Matthew 25:40 (“Whatever you did for the least…”). Pax Christi: international Catholic peace movement working for disarmament and nonviolent conflict resolution, grounded in the Beatitude (Matthew 5:9). Corrymeela: ecumenical reconciliation community in Northern Ireland, bringing Catholics and Protestants together, grounded in 2 Corinthians 5:18.
exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question about mission or the work of a named Catholic organisation, always name the organisation AND explain its theological grounding. For the SVP: cite Matthew 25:40. For Pax Christi: cite Matthew 5:9 (“Blessed are the peacemakers”). For Corrymeela: cite 2 Corinthians 5:18 (ministry of reconciliation). A source without development earns partial marks; a source with a full explanation of how it motivates the organisation earns top-band marks.

For the 12-mark Evaluate (e.g. “Mission is the most important Catholic activity today”), you need arguments on both sides. Arguments FOR mission: the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19); Catholic identity is inherently missionary. Arguments AGAINST: the Eucharist is ‘source and summit’; social action (CAFOD, SVP) may do more immediate good; non-religious view that proselytisation interferes with individual freedom of belief. Your JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION must choose a side and explain why.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mission is the task given by Jesus in Matthew 28:19–20 (the Great Commission) to share the Gospel with all nations. Catholics in Britain today engage in evangelism through faith courses, parish outreach and community service. The challenge in a secular society is to share the faith winsmomely without coercion.
  • The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP) is a lay Catholic organisation present in 153 countries, providing direct person-to-person service of the poor based on Matthew 25:40. Local parish conferences visit the elderly, housebound and isolated, embodying the Catholic conviction that serving the poor is serving Christ.
  • Pax Christi is an international Catholic peace movement working for disarmament and nonviolent conflict resolution, grounded in Matthew 5:9. Corrymeela is an ecumenical reconciliation community in Northern Ireland that has brought Catholic and Protestant communities together since 1965, grounded in 2 Corinthians 5:18 (the ministry of reconciliation).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the work of the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP)?
A) Running a network of Catholic secondary schools across Britain
B) Providing person-to-person service of the poor through local parish groups in 153 countries
C) Organising pilgrimage tours to Lourdes and Walsingham
D) Campaigning for nuclear disarmament and international peace
practice_questions.marks: B) Providing person-to-person service of the poor through local parish groups in 153 countries [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the command Jesus gave to his disciples in Matthew 28:19-20 that forms the basis of Catholic mission.
practice_questions.marks: The Great Commission [1 mark]. Accept 'go and make disciples of all nations' or a paraphrase indicating the command to spread the Gospel.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Catholics in Britain today carry out mission and evangelism.
For each way, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Catholics run faith exploration courses such as RCIA (Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults) or Alpha — these invite people who are not Catholic or who are returning to faith to explore Christianity in a welcoming setting, responding to Jesus's command to 'go and make disciples' (Matthew 28:19).
- Through the work of organisations like the SVP, Catholics embody the Gospel by serving the poor and marginalised in their local communities; this demonstrates the faith in action rather than just in words, and can draw people toward the Church.
- Individual Catholics may speak openly about their faith in workplaces and schools, or invite friends to Mass — a form of personal evangelism that many parish missions encourage.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the work of Pax Christi or Corrymeela is important for Catholics.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons for either Pax Christi or Corrymeela (or one each); named source integrated and developed (e.g. Matthew 5:9, Matthew 5:44, 2 Corinthians 5:18, Gaudium et Spes); both reasons clearly connected to Catholic belief or practice.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate; source cited but not fully developed.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic relevant point; no source.

Acceptable points for Pax Christi:
- Pax Christi works for disarmament because Catholic teaching holds that nuclear weapons threaten the God-given dignity of all human life; Jesus's Beatitude 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God' (Matthew 5:9) gives Catholics a clear mandate to oppose warfare and militarism.
- Pax Christi's campaigns also draw on the just war tradition: Catholic theology has always held that war must meet strict conditions to be morally justified; nuclear weapons, which cannot discriminate between combatants and civilians, fail to meet these conditions.

Acceptable points for Corrymeela:
- Corrymeela has brought Catholic and Protestant communities in Northern Ireland together since 1965, building relationships across a divide that has resulted in violence and death; this expresses the Catholic commitment to reconciliation as a practical Gospel imperative — 'God gave us the ministry of reconciliation' (2 Corinthians 5:18).
- The willingness of Catholics to work alongside Protestants in Corrymeela reflects the Catholic teaching on ecumenism (work for Christian unity) and on the dignity of every person, regardless of denomination.

practice_questions.text:
'Mission and evangelism is the most important task of Catholics in Britain today.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; Catholic teaching on mission (Matthew 28:19), the Eucharist as source and summit, social action (SVP, CAFOD); non-religious view on evangelism as interference; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source cited; conclusion reached.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20) is Jesus's final command to his disciples — it is the last thing he said before the Ascension; if Catholics take the words of Christ seriously, mission must be a high priority.
- Without mission, the Church would decline and eventually disappear; Catholics have a duty to share the Good News they have received so others can experience the grace and salvation Jesus offers.
- Pope Francis has consistently called for a 'missionary Church' that goes out to the margins — this is the Pope's own stated priority for the Church in the twenty-first century.

Arguments against:
- Catholic theology insists that the Eucharist is 'the source and summit of Christian life'; without worship, sacramental life and prayer, mission has no foundation — the most important task may be maintaining the community of faith.
- The work of the SVP, CAFOD and Pax Christi arguably does more immediate good for the world's poor and suffering than evangelism; many Catholics today see social action as their primary vocation.
- From a non-religious perspective, evangelism that aims to convert others may interfere with their freedom of belief and conscience; in a pluralist society, building peace and justice across religious boundaries (as Corrymeela does) may be more important than denominational expansion.

Conclusion: Candidates may argue either side. A strong conclusion might acknowledge that for Catholic theology, mission, worship and social action are inseparable — each nourishes the others — but that the Great Commission gives mission a foundational importance that cannot be set aside without abandoning a core Gospel imperative.

practice_questions.text: Jerome is a member of his local SVP conference in a Catholic parish in London. Give two things he might do as part of his work for the SVP.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid point (up to 2 marks total).
Acceptable points include:
- Visiting elderly or housebound parishioners to offer company and practical help.
- Delivering food parcels or clothing to people in need in the local community.
- Running or supporting a lunch club or drop-in for lonely or isolated people.
- Helping someone in financial difficulty to access benefits or emergency support.
- Bringing Holy Communion to those who cannot attend Mass.
